This document presents Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG), by Yuntong Hu, Zhihan Lei, Zheng Zhang, Bo Pan, Chen Ling, and Liang Zhao of the Department of Computer Science at Emory University. GRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation for networked documents represented as textual graphs, whose nodes and edges carry text. Rather than retrieving isolated documents by text similarity, it retrieves query-relevant textual subgraphs so that Large Language Models can use both content and graph topology for multi-hop reasoning. The paper first situates GRAG among prompt tuning, LLM-based graph work, and graph retrieval methods, arguing that text-trained LLMs do not inherently capture complex graph structure. It formalizes the task as finding an optimal textual subgraph for a query and supplying it to an LLM to improve output relevance. GRAG’s retrieval uses a divide-and-conquer approach: it indexes and ranks K-hop ego-graphs with a pre-trained language model, selects the top-N neighborhoods by cosine similarity to the query, merges them, and applies soft pruning. Soft pruning uses two Multilayer Perceptrons to assign query-dependent scaling factors to nodes and edges; elements less relevant to the query are masked toward zero. This produces a tailored subgraph with linear complexity. For generation, GRAG creates complementary views. Its text view turns retrieved ego-graphs into hierarchical descriptions using BFS and pre-order traversal while retaining extra edges. Its graph view uses a Graph Neural Network and learned relevance scaling factors to encode the pruned subgraph, then aligns graph embeddings with the language model token space. These graph embeddings are combined with query and description text embeddings to guide generation through hard and soft prompts. Experiments on GraphQA, using WebQSP and ExplaGraphs, report that GRAG outperforms standard RAG retrievers, LLM baselines, and fine-tuned Llama2-7b models on reported metrics. Ablations indicate that graph-aware retrieval, graph encoding, pruning, and descriptions matter; 2-hop ego-graphs generally beat 1-hop graphs, while excessive retrieval adds irrelevant information. The conclusion emphasizes stronger detailed multi-hop reasoning and lower training cost because frozen LLMs can outperform fine-tuned models. The main limitation is dependence on effective initial node ranking and pruning when graph structure or node importance is hard to estimate.

l: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG) is a computational framework and Retrieval-Augmented Generation extension for networked documents and graph-based scenarios. It treats documents as textual graphs, considering graph context in both retrieval and generation to improve Large Language Models’ generation and multi-hop graph reasoning. Given a query, its objective is to retrieve an optimal relevant textual subgraph and incorporate that subgraph’s textual and topological information into an LLM. Rather than exhaustively searching subgraphs, an NP-hard challenge, GRAG uses a divide-and-conquer retrieval-then-pruning process: it directly retrieves important ego-graphs, merges the top-N relevant ego-graphs, and applies soft pruning to reduce redundant graph information while approximately preserving the relevant subgraph structure. The retrieved graph is represented through two complementary views: a text view, supplied with hard prompts, and a graph view, encoded by a graph encoder and supplied with soft prompts. It also uses hierarchical graph descriptions of retrieved textual subgraphs, enabling graph context-aware generation through joint textual and topological information. Across evaluated graph reasoning benchmarks, GRAG significantly outperforms tested RAG retrievers, RAG-based LLMs, LLM baselines, and a fine-tuned LLM when using a frozen LLM; reported improvements include WebQSP Hit@1 from 0.4148 to 0.7236 and ExplaGraphs accuracy from 0.3394 to 0.9223 without LLM fine-tuning. It can reduce training cost and has cross-dataset transferability of learned textual graph encoding capabilities. Its limitation is that retrieval may be suboptimal when graph structure or node importance is difficult to estimate.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a generation method that integrates external data retrieval into the generative process, helping Large Language Models produce more relevant answers and reduce factual errors. Traditional retrieval focuses on individual documents through text similarity, which falls short for networked documents; Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation extends it for graph-based scenarios.

l: textual graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual graphs are networked documents, common in citation graphs, social media, and knowledge graphs, that may contain social media postings, research papers, knowledge items, and product reviews. They matter because network information, including citations, social interactions, entity relations, and purchasing links, provides context for retrieval, generation, and prompting Large Language Models, beyond retrieval of individual documents. Formally, a textual graph is G = (V, E, {Tn}n∈V, {Te}e∈E): a graph whose nodes and edges have natural-language attributes. For textual subgraph retrieval, it is represented through graph and text views to preserve connected structure and narrated connections. Retrieved ego-graphs can become hierarchical descriptions while retaining information for lossless conversion between K-hop ego-graphs and text descriptions. Textual graphs provide the scenarios and contexts for GRAG, particularly when detailed, multi-hop reasoning is required.

l: textual subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual subgraphs are subgraph structures of a textual graph, containing selected nodes and edges with their natural-language features and networked documents’ textual and topological relationships. They matter because GRAG retrieves them rather than discrete entities, preserving relationships and improving retrieval precision, robustness, and coverage. GRAG uses divide-and-conquer to approximate an optimal query-relevant subgraph in linear time, then supplies it to LLMs.

l: Large Language Models, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large Language Models are language models trained on large text corpora to develop language understanding. They provide text embeddings for textual node and edge attributes and contextual reasoning that supports graph reasoning and zero-shot graph answering. They demonstrate reasoning capabilities on graph-based data, yet textual training does not inherently provide understanding of complex graph-structured data, and they can make factual errors because of training-data limits and no real-time knowledge. Through GRAG, complementary text and graph views supply textual and graph information, helping them comprehend and use graph context more effectively for responses involving networked documents.

l: divide-and-conquer strategy, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The divide-and-conquer strategy is a retrieval strategy for efficient textual subgraph retrieval. It treats a retrieved subgraph as a union of partial neighborhoods around important nodes, searches for important ego-graphs, ranks them to select top-ranked key nodes, and retrieves relevant ego-graphs first. It then uses soft pruning to refine and union K-hop ego-graphs, approximating an optimal subgraph in linear time.

l: optimal subgraph structure, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The optimal textual subgraph is a query-tailored union of selected, adaptively masked node neighborhoods from graph G. Its information is concatenated with query q for LLMθ, aiming to maximize generation quality and produce answers aligned with expectations. Although directly finding the optimum is NP-hard, it is approximated through neighborhood selection and merging, and retrieved by divide-and-conquer with linear construction complexity.

l: graph context-aware generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph context-aware generation incorporates textual graphs into Large Language Models through complementary text and graph views, helping them use graph context more effectively; GRAG provides an effective framework for this area.

l: Text View of Textual Graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Text View of Textual Graphs is a complementary view of a textual graph used by GRAG. It converts retrieved textual subgraphs into hierarchical text descriptions through graph and tree traversals, retaining narrated connections as well as textual and topological information. From subgraph retrieval to generation, it concatenates the query with the hierarchical description as a hard prompt for the language model.

l: graph multi-hop reasoning tasks, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph multi-hop reasoning tasks are empirical benchmarks and a reasoning requirement used to evaluate Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation on textual graphs. Across experiments including WebQSP, they compare GRAG with RAG retrievers and Large Language Model baselines. GRAG significantly outperforms these methods; even a frozen Large Language Model with GRAG exceeds a fine-tuned Large Language Model. The results emphasize retrieving and encoding graph structure over text retrieval or fine-tuning alone.

l: graph-structured data, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph-structured data contains complex structural information that is not explicitly represented in ordinary textual data. Retrieval methods incorporate textual and topological information to better capture its structural relationships.

l: textual subgraph retrieval, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual subgraph retrieval is a high-dimensional retrieval problem involving textual node and edge features. In GRAG, it aims to find a subgraph maximizing generation quality through divide-and-conquer: retrieve and rank K-hop ego-graphs, then refine and union selected neighborhoods with graph soft pruning. It avoids exhaustive subgraph search, but depends on accurate initial node ranking and pruning, and may suffer when structure or node importance is hard to estimate.

A K-hop ego-graph is a neighborhood centered on an ego node, assigned a unique identifier, encoded as a graph embedding, and retrieved to constrain search space. Unlike a tree, it can contain additional intra-level or cross-level edges. For textual representation, it is divided into a BFS-derived tree rooted at the ego node and a remaining edge set, then described hierarchically. It supports divide-and-conquer textual subgraph retrieval; on WebQSP, retrieved 2-hop ego-graphs outperform 1-hop ones at equal retrieval counts, though too many may introduce irrelevant information. Larger-than-3-hop ego-graphs are subject to oversmoothing.

l: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning is a method that minimizes irrelevant and redundant nodes and edges in retrieved subgraphs, producing a query-tailored optimal subgraph structure with linear complexity. During graph-token encoding, it removes irrelevant entities; with K-hop ego-graphs in divide-and-conquer, it approximates the optimal textual subgraph and is especially crucial for dense graphs.

l: NP-hard problem, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: describes optimal textual subgraph retrieval The NP-hard problem is the direct optimization of a textual subgraph to maximize generation quality. The method works around it by approximating the objective as a sum of scores for individual ego-graphs.

l: hierarchical text descriptions, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Hierarchical text descriptions generated from retrieved textual subgraphs use graph algorithms to encode topological information as hard prompts. They are important for LLM graph-related generation: removing them substantially lowers WebQSP Hit@1 to 0.4496, despite retained textual node and edge attributes and soft graph tokens.

l: hard prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: retain how connections are narrated Hard prompts provide text-token representations of retrieved textual subgraphs to the Large Language Model. In GRAG, they are formed from hierarchical text descriptions that preserve topological information in textual form.

l: soft prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Soft prompts are graph-token representations of retrieved textual subgraphs, generated by graph encoders to preserve textual connections and original parameters while enabling task-specific adaptations.

l: graph tokens, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph tokens encode graph context for the LLM. They are most effective when irrelevant entities are pruned and when textual attributes are also supplied.

l: Graph Neural Network, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph Neural Network is a graph encoder that encodes topological information and improves graph-context comprehension. It unfolds by using learned node and edge relevance scaling factors to control message passing, then supplying graph context to an LLM through graph tokens; removing it reduces WebQSP Hit@1 from 0.7275 to 0.5835.

l: Prompt Tuning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Prompt Tuning is an automated method that modifies inputs without updating model parameters, using task-specific soft prompt embeddings to guide responses and adapt prompts for multi-modal contexts.

l: Low-rank Adaptation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Low-rank Adaptation is a fine-tuning method used on an LLM baseline; in experiments, it yields large gains alone on ExplaGraphs but marginal gains when GRAG is used.
Fine-tuning updates model parameters, substantially improving standalone LLM performance on smaller ExplaGraphs graphs but offering limited benefits on larger WebQSP graphs and additional GRAG gains.

l: knowledge graph question answering, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LLMs are applied to graph-related tasks including node and edge attribute classification, knowledge graph creation, graph reasoning, and zero-shot graph answering. Knowledge graph question answering is represented by the WebQSP dataset. The experiments use F1 Score, Hit@1, and Recall to measure performance.

l: graph reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LLM contextual reasoning capabilities benefit graph reasoning. However, text-based training alone does not inherently provide the ability to reason about complex graph-structured data.

l: topological information, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual data lacks explicit topological information, limiting LLM understanding of complex graph structures. Graph prompt tuning and retrieval methods help introduce or use topological information.

l: graph prompt tuning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a tool [for helping LLMs process and comprehend topological information] Graph prompt tuning has recently emerged as a tool for helping LLMs process and comprehend topological information.

l: Retrieval on Graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a research area Retrieval on graphs includes methods that retrieve relevant nodes, triples, paths, or communities for answering questions. These methods can combine QA context with retrieved graph elements and use textual and topological information to capture structural relationships.

Enhanced retrieval processes select graph information relevant to a query, including nodes, edges, triples, paths, or communities, while incorporating textual and topological information. Retrieval is necessary because providing all graph text yields suboptimal LLM performance. Selecting subgraphs and using topology during generation mitigates redundant graph information and improves performance.

l: reasoning chains, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Reasoning chains simplify some retrieval problems by retrieving the path from a question to its target entity.

l: topological information in graph-structured data, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval methods can incorporate topological information in graph-structured data alongside textual information. This allows models to better capture structural relationships within the graph.

l: graph G, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: G is a textual graph with finite V and E; S(G) contains subgraphs formed from their subsets.

The query is provided over a textual graph and encoded by a pre-trained language model as a query embedding. It measures semantic relevance to K-hop ego-graphs through cosine similarity and serves as the reference for pruning distant entities. Combined with an optimal textual subgraph, it guides retrieval and generation, appearing in the hard prompt with the hierarchical description.

l: Large Language Models, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large Language Models are parameterized by θ and generate final output sequences token by token from a query, optimal textual subgraph, hierarchical textual-graph description, and aligned graph embeddings. They demonstrate reasoning on graphs, especially hierarchical texts. Through GRAG, a frozen LLM receives query-relevant textual subgraphs, enhancing generation and potentially outperforming fine-tuned LLMs at reduced training cost.

l: final output sequence Y, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Y is a generation output with probability distribution pθ(Y | [q, G]), produced autoregressively by a large language model, conditioning each token on prior tokens and concatenated graph and text embeddings.

l: retrieval-then-pruning approach, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The retrieval-then-pruning approach restricts search to |V| ego-graphs, retrieves and ranks promising candidates, retains top ones, then prunes redundant nodes and edges to yield approximately optimal subgraph structure.

l: Graph View of Textual Graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph View of Textual Graphs is a complementary view of a textual graph in GRAG. It learns graph representations as soft prompts to preserve connections among texts. Beginning with a soft pruned subgraph, it uses a Graph Neural Network and learned relevance scaling factors to control message passing, encode topology, and align graph embeddings with the language model’s token space.

l: key nodes, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Key nodes, selected as top-ranked, form the retrieved textual subgraph’s backbone by determining which partial neighborhoods are combined.

l: textual subgraph indexing, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: indexes ego-graph [each K-hop ego-graph is assigned a unique identifier] Textual subgraph indexing pools the encoded textual attributes of the nodes and edges in each K-hop ego-graph. The resulting graph embeddings are stored for the subsequent retrieval process.

converts text attributes of nodes and edges [into embeddings] The pre-trained language model converts node and edge text attributes into embeddings for textual subgraph indexing. The same encoder is also used to encode the query.

l: graph embedding, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A graph embedding represents a subgraph and is obtained by mean pooling pre-trained language model embeddings of its node and edge text attributes into dimension d.

l: textual subgraph ranking, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual subgraph ranking uses the same PLM encoder to compare a query with each K-hop ego-graph by cosine similarity, returning top-N relevant subgraphs as S_N(G).

l: subgraphs retrieved from graph G, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Subgraphs retrieved from graph G may retain irrelevant nodes and edges, so the N most semantically relevant are selected. During generation, a retrieved subgraph provides hierarchical description and graph representation: its text becomes a hard prompt and its structure a soft prompt.

l: irrelevant nodes and edges, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Irrelevant nodes and edges may negatively impact the final generation. Their influence is reduced through adaptive scaling, with entities farther from the query being more effectively masked.

l: Multilayer Perceptrons, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: learn scaling factor [based on the distance between nodes & edges and the query] Two Multilayer Perceptrons learn scaling factors from the element-wise distance between node or edge representations and the query representation. One processes node representations and the other processes edge representations.

l: relevance scaling factors, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Relevance scaling factors, learned by two Multilayer Perceptrons from distances between nodes, edges, and a query, control graph-encoder message passing by scaling node features and edge attributes; they adaptively mask tokens, approaching zero farther from the query.

l: adaptively masked subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Adaptively masked subgraphs use learned scalar masks on nodes and edges, then merge selected subgraphs into an optimal query-tailored structure.

l: Textual Graph Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: provides_views_of textual graph [two complementary views] Textual Graph Augmented Generation provides large language models with two complementary views of a textual graph: a text view and a graph view.

l: Generation Phase, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Generation Phase is guided by the retrieved subgraph and original query, combining aligned graph and text embeddings before feeding them into the language model’s transformer layers.
The tree is a partially ordered set rooted at the ego node and is obtained from an ego-graph using BFS. Its nodes and edges are organized through pre-order traversal.

l: hierarchical description, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A hierarchical description is a representation that preserves textual and topological information, enabling lossless conversion between K-hop ego-graphs and text descriptions. It is created by pre-order tree traversal, appending node and edge texts through a relation template and inserting remaining-edge texts.

l: hard prompt, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The hard prompt concatenates a query with a hierarchical description of a textual subgraph as [q, Dg], then a language model’s text embedder converts it into text embeddings.

l: soft pruned subgraph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: provides soft prompt [as its learned representation] The soft pruned subgraph is represented as a soft prompt to reduce the influence of irrelevant entities during generation. Its message passing is controlled through learned relevance scaling factors.
aligns graph embeddings [with the LLM tokens] MLPϕ3 aligns the graph embeddings produced by GNNΦ with the text-vector space of LLMθ. Its output has dimension dLLM.

l: graph embeddings, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph embeddings have dimension dLLM after alignment, aggregate retrieved-subgraph topology to enhance structural awareness, then are aligned by MLPϕ3 and concatenated with text embeddings for language-model generation.

l: text embeddings, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: represent hard prompt [produced by the text embedder of LLMθ] The text embeddings are produced by the text embedder of LLMθ from the hard prompt [q, Dg]. They are concatenated with the aligned graph embeddings for generation.

is_a benchmark GraphQA is the benchmark used to evaluate graph-related question answering in these experiments. Its datasets contain textual graphs paired with questions and answers that require comprehension of graph context.
WebQSP is a large-scale, multi-hop knowledge graph question answering dataset, averaging 4,700 graphs and 1,370.89 nodes; it is evaluated with graph, edge, token, and GRAG Hit@1 results.

is_a common-sense reasoning dataset [focused on predicting positions in debates] ExplaGraphs is evaluated as a common-sense reasoning dataset focused on predicting positions in debates. GRAG achieves 0.9223 accuracy without fine-tuning and 0.9274 with LoRA fine-tuning.

uses retrieval [to provide external knowledge to an LLM] RAG with standard text retrievers improves LLM performance over using the LLM alone, but its text-focused retrieval does not incorporate graph topology. The tested RAG approaches generally perform below GRAG.
G-Retriever aggregates topological information as soft prompts and outperforms comparison retrievers, but omits topology during retrieval; GRAG performs better by directly retrieving subgraphs.

is_used_as LLM [in the experiments] Llama2-7b is the LLM used in the experiments, including the frozen and LoRA fine-tuned baselines. Its 7B version slightly outperforms the 13B version without retrieval on both ExplaGraphs and WebQSP.
is_a evaluation metric [used for WebQSP] Hit@1 is one of the primary evaluation metrics for WebQSP. GRAG raises Hit@1 from 0.4148 for the LLM-only baseline to 0.7236, while GRAGLoRA reaches 0.7275.

l: common-sense reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a task [on ExplaGraphs] Common-sense reasoning is evaluated with ExplaGraphs, which focuses on positions in debates. GRAG substantially improves accuracy on this task, including when its graph encoding capabilities are transferred from WebQSP.

l: ablation study, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: evaluates GRAG components The ablation study evaluates the effects of retrieval, the graph encoder, soft pruning, and graph descriptions on WebQSP. It finds that removing graph descriptions causes the largest reported decline, followed by removing soft pruning, the graph encoder, and retrieval.

l: initial node ranking and pruning mechanism, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: has_quality quality [quality affects textual subgraph retrieval efficiency] The initial node ranking and pruning mechanism affects the efficiency of GRAG's textual subgraph retrieval. Poor estimation of graph structure or node importance can lead to suboptimal retrieval performance.
